{{nihongo|'''Ooi Shrine'''|大井神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Tanba Province]].

'''Ooi Shrine''' (おおいじんじゃ) is a Shinto shrine in Oi-cho, {{ill|Kameoka, Kyoto|ar|كاميوكا|azb|کامه‌اوکا، کیوتو|ce|Камеока|ceb|Kameoka-shi|cs|Kameoka|de|Kameoka|eo|Kameoka|es|Kameoka (Kioto)|eu|Kameoka (Kyoto)|fa|کامه‌اوکا، کیوتو|fi|Kameoka|fr|Kameoka|gl|Kameoka|id|Kameoka, Kyōto|it|Kameoka|ja|亀岡市|ko|가메오카시|lt|Kameoka|mg|Kameoka|my|ခမဲအိုခမြို့၊ ကျိုတို|mzn|کامه‌اوکا، کیوتو|nl|Kameoka|pl|Kameoka|pt|Kameoka|ro|Kameoka|ru|Камеока|simple|Kameoka, Kyoto|sv|Kameoka|tg|Камеока|th|คาเมโอกะ|tl|Kameoka, Kyoto|tr|Kameoka|tt|Камеока|uk|Камеока|ur|کامی اوکا، کیوٹو|vi|Kameoka, Kyōto|war|Kameoka, Kyoto|zh|龜岡市|zh_classical|龜岡市|zh_min_nan|Kameoka-chhī|zh_yue|龜岡|qid=Q633996}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|Q120730|qid=Q120730}}. It is a shikinaisha and was formerly ranked as a gosha.

=== History ===
=== Traditions ===
; Carp legend
A shrine tradition says that in 702 deities from {{ill|Matsunoo Taisha|Q710302|qid=Q710302}} traveled upstream on the Oi River, first riding a turtle; when blocked by rapids near Hozu, they switched to a carp and reached Ariimoto-buchi in Kameoka, where a shrine was founded and later moved to the present site.<ref name="chimei">''Kyoto-fu no Chimei,'' Ooi Shrine section.</ref><ref name="yuisho">Shrine origin record.</ref>

From this legend, carp are treated as sacred messengers at this shrine. Parishioners traditionally avoid eating carp and do not display carp streamers at Boys' Festival.

; Origin of the name "Ooi"
A tradition says the Kameoka Basin was once a lake ("Ni no Umi"). After it drained, a large spring/well remained here, never drying even in droughts, and this "great well" became the origin of the name "Ooi." Because loss of this spring was feared to bring either flooding or drought, the well deity Kimata-no-kami (Mii-no-kami) was invited and enshrined.<ref name="yuisho"/><ref name="setsumei">On-site explanatory board.</ref>

The shrine explains that its name derives from "great well" (oi) rather than from the river weir (oi) near Arashiyama.

=== Historical outline ===
Shrine tradition attributes foundation to an imperial order of Empress Genmei in 710. The shrine appears in the ''Engishiki Jinmyocho'' as "Ooi Shrine, Kuwata District, Tanba Province." It burned in warfare in 1576 and was rebuilt in 1584 by order of {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|qid=Q187550}}; construction commissioner {{ill|Katagiri Katsumoto|Q1882775|qid=Q1882775}} is said to have donated a plaque reading "Shoichii Ooi Daimyojin."

In 1873 it was ranked gosha, recognized as a shikinaisha in June 1877, and designated as a shinsen-heihaku offering shrine in March 1907. Ahead of the 1300th anniversary in 2010, the honden underwent full restoration (completed October 2009).

=== Precinct ===
An Amida Buddha statue in the precinct is said to be the former honji-butsu of Toko-ji, once the shrine's betto temple.

=== Festivals ===
* Monthly festival (1st of each month)
* New Year festival (Jan 1)
* Traffic safety prayer (Jan 3)
* Tondo fire rite (Jan 15)
* Kinen-sai (spring equinox in March)
* Summer purification (Jun 30)
* Flower/Tachibana dedication rite (Aug 19) - Kyoto Prefecture designated intangible folk cultural property
* Grand festival / shinko-sai (Oct 16)
: Horse-racing dedication (kurabe-uma) by parishioners in warrior attire is held at adjacent grounds.
* Shichi-go-san prayers (November)
* Niiname-sai (Nov 23)
* Year-end purification (Dec 31)

=== Cultural properties ===
=== Kyoto Prefecture designated cultural property ===
* Intangible folk cultural property: Ooi Shrine Tachibana rite (designated April 19, 1991)
